blocks.text: A cheap Christmas-light string on a stall in Balogun market goes completely dark if one bulb blows, because the lamps are in series: one gap stops the whole current. The string of bulbs in a properly wired parlour stays on when one lamp fails, because those lamps sit in parallel across the 220 V PHCN supply. Same bulbs, two different networks.

blocks.markdown:
Resistors (or lamps, or any other loads) can be joined **in series** or **in parallel**, and the two arrangements behave very differently.

**Series** — a single path. The same current $I$ flows through every resistor. The potential differences add up to the supply p.d. The effective resistance is the ordinary sum:

$$R = R_1 + R_2 + R_3 + \cdots$$

The effective resistance is **always larger than the largest** individual resistor.

**Parallel** — several paths between the same two points. Each branch has the **same** potential difference. The currents add: $I = I_1 + I_2 + I_3$. The effective resistance satisfies

$$\frac{1}{R} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} + \frac{1}{R_3} + \cdots$$

For two resistors this rearranges to $R = \frac{R_1 R_2}{R_1 + R_2}$. The effective resistance is **always smaller than the smallest** individual resistor.

blocks.title: A cell with internal resistance
blocks.text: A real cell is not a perfect source. It has an electromotive force E (the p.d. across its terminals on open circuit) and a small internal resistance r. When a current I is drawn, some p.d. is lost inside the cell as Ir, so the terminal potential difference is V = E − Ir. Equivalently, E = I(R + r), where R is the external resistance.

blocks.latex: E = I(R + r) \qquad V = E - Ir = IR

blocks.title: Series–parallel combination and a cell
blocks.prompt: Two resistors of 6.0 Ω and 3.0 Ω are connected in parallel. This combination is then joined in series with a 4.0 Ω resistor and a cell of e.m.f. 6.0 V and internal resistance 0.50 Ω. Calculate (a) the effective external resistance, (b) the current drawn from the cell, (c) the terminal p.d. of the cell.

steps.text: Add the series 4.0 Ω resistor to get the external resistance.
(b) The total resistance in the circuit is R + r. Find the current from E = I(R + r).
(c) Terminal p.d. is the p.d. across the external circuit, V = E − Ir.

blocks.markdown:
### Current and p.d. in each branch

Once you have the current leaving the cell, push it through the network one junction at a time.

- In **series**, current is the same; p.d. across each resistor is $V_n = I R_n$. The larger resistor takes the larger share of the voltage.
- In **parallel**, p.d. is the same; current in each branch is $I_n = V / R_n$. The **smaller** resistor takes the **larger** current.

On **open circuit** ($I = 0$) the terminal p.d. equals the e.m.f.: $V = E$. On **short circuit** ($R = 0$) the current is $I = E/r$ and the terminal p.d. falls to zero.

items: Reduce any parallel groups to a single equivalent resistor.
Add series resistors (including r) to get the total resistance seen by the cell.
Find the cell current from I = E / (R + r).
Work backwards: terminal p.d. V = E − Ir, then split that p.d. or current at each junction.

blocks.title: WAEC and JAMB tip
blocks.text: For two resistors in parallel, the effective value is the product divided by the sum — but only for exactly two. For three, you must add the three reciprocals. Never add parallel resistors as if they were in series. And do not forget r: using I = E/R instead of I = E/(R + r) is the most common lost mark on internal-resistance questions.

points: Series: same current, p.d.s add, R = R₁ + R₂. Effective R is larger than the largest resistor.
Parallel: same p.d., currents add, 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂. Effective R is smaller than the smallest resistor.
The smaller parallel branch carries the larger current; the larger series resistor takes the larger p.d.
A cell has e.m.f. E and internal resistance r. The current is I = E/(R + r) and the terminal p.d. is V = E − Ir = IR.
On open circuit V = E; on short circuit I = E/r and V = 0.
